title: Neighborhood Fab-Commons: Custom, Repairable Goods Made Two Blocks Away
tagline: Fixtureless metal printers, 3D zero-waste looms, CNC timber cells, and robotic unscrewers turn vacant strip malls into circular neighborhood microfactories.
cynicBelief: Consumer goods will always come from 8,000-mile container ships with glued-shut planned obsolescence so a broken $2 plastic latch forces a $700 washer into the dump.
breakthroughCounter: Divergent 3D generative aluminum-alloy nodes (zero $50M stamping dies), high-speed Prusa/Bambu polymer farms, Shima Seiki 28-minute zero-waste 3D knitters, WikiHouse CNC timber cells, and Apple Daisy / Molg 200-device/hr unscrewing robots fit a multi-product circular factory inside one vacant storefront.
socialNormShift: Inspired by France's Repairability Index, EU Digital Product Passports, Sweden's tax-free repairs, and Barcelona's public Ateneus Fab Labs, towns co-locate Tool Libraries & Fab-Commons where a public library card unlocks $4.50 15-minute spare parts and $65 custom kids' prosthetics.

humanStory.snippet: Inside a sunlit former electronics big-box store, Ingrid prints a $4.50 carbon-PEEK cam from her 14-year-old dishwasher's QR Passport in 12 minutes, 11-year-old Samir gets a custom-scanned $65 bionic socket before lunch, and Freja slots recycled-can aluminum nodes into a cargo e-bike.

quote.text: Instead of shipping atoms across oceans in container ships, global Fab Labs let cities transmit bits at the speed of light and fabricate locally from circular materials.
